exercises.approach: Call plot_ly on d with x = ~x, y = ~observed, type = "scatter" and mode = "markers", and name the trace Observed.
exercises.why: The three pairs (1, 2), (2, 4) and (3, 3) are separate measurements. Markers show each one without suggesting that the response moved smoothly from one input to the next.
exercises.wrong: Drawing the observations with add_lines. The segment from 4 down to 3 then reads as a measured decline between inputs 2 and 3, which no observation supports.

exercises.approach: Add the rule with add_lines(p, y = ~rule, name = "Rule: 2x"), which reuses x from the plot_ly call.
exercises.why: The rule column holds 2, 4 and 6, so the line agrees with the observations at inputs 1 and 2 and sits 3 above the observed value at input 3. A separate named trace keeps that modeled comparison distinct from the data.
exercises.wrong: Adding the rule as a second unnamed marker trace. It shares the marker style, and the legend falls back to a generic trace label, so a reader cannot tell which points were measured.

exercises.approach: Pass xaxis = list(title = "Input") and yaxis = list(title = "Response") to layout.
exercises.why: Without them plotly titles the axes from the formulas, so the y axis would read observed even though it also carries the rule. layout changes the labels without touching any trace values.
exercises.wrong: Renaming the data columns to carry display text, such as a column called Response value. Every formula and check then has to quote that name, and the label is still tied to one trace rather than the axis.
exercises.verify: `as.numeric(built$x$data[[1]]$y)` still returns 2, 4, 3 after layout, and the rendered figure shows Input and Response as axis titles.

exercises.approach: Reorder whole rows with `unsorted[order(unsorted$x), ]` before using a trace that connects points in row order, such as mode = "lines" or add_paths.
exercises.why: The rows arrive as x = 3, 1, 2 with y = 6, 2, 4, so a row order path runs from (3, 6) back to (1, 2) and then to (2, 4). add_lines sorts by x for you, but the other connectors do not, so the order should be declared rather than assumed.
exercises.wrong: Sorting only the x column with sort(unsorted$x). The pairs become (1, 6), (2, 2) and (3, 4), so the line connects values that were never observed together.

exercises.approach: Map category to x and count to y on the counts table with type = "bar", and keep zero on the y axis with `rangemode = "tozero"`.
exercises.why: counts already holds one row per category with heights 2, 1 and 3. A bar trace draws those values as given, and the character categories keep the order A, B, C in which they appear.
exercises.wrong: Using type = "histogram" with x = ~category. The histogram counts rows, and each category occurs once in counts, so every bar has height 1.

exercises.approach: Record what each check covers: plotly_build confirms the trace values, print(p) and print(bar) request the two figures for capture, and the browser view confirms what students see.
exercises.why: The built specification proves two traces with 2, 4, 3 and 2, 4, 6 and a bar trace with 2, 1, 3. It cannot show whether plotly.js loads on the classroom page, or whether hover, zoom and the legend respond.
exercises.wrong: Treating the closing cat line as proof that the interactive page works. The script reaches that line even when the widget later fails to load its JavaScript in the browser.
exercises.verify: The reference prints r-057 reference checks passed, and a separate browser session shows both figures with working hover text.
